stem: Which of these are quadratic equations?

diag.0: degree 1 — an equation having an $x$ in it is not the same as being quadratic
diag.3: $x$ is in the exponent, not the base. That is exponential.
diag.4: degree 3. Having powers is not the same as being quadratic.

miss.2: It is quadratic: expanding gives $x^{2}+3x-4=0$. The degree is read after the equation is written as $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$.

stem: The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown. What are the solutions of $f(x)=0$?

options.v: You cannot tell without the equation

diag.1: reads “$f(x)=0$” as an instruction to set $x$ to zero
diag.2: gives where it crosses the $y$-axis instead of the $x$-axis
diag.3: The graph is enough: the solutions of $f(x)=0$ are the $x$-values where the curve meets the $x$-axis, here $x=-1$ and $x=4$.

stem: $f(x)=(x-2)(x+5)$. Without expanding, where does the graph cross the $x$-axis?

options.v: You have to expand it first

diag.1: reads the numbers in the brackets as the roots without changing sign
diag.3: $(x-2)(x+5)=0$ when one factor is zero, so $x=2$ or $x=-5$. Expanding is not needed.

stem: A student solves $2x^{2}-3x-5=0$ with the formula. They write $a=2$, $b=3$, $c=5$, reach $\sqrt{9-40}$, and conclude there are no real solutions.

options.v: Nothing — there really are no real solutions

diag.1: $2a=2(2)=4$ is correct. This looks wrong only if $a$ is misread.
diag.2: $9+40=49$ is the right value, but it follows only from $c=-5$. With $c=5$ as written, $b^{2}-4ac=9-40$.
diag.3: the roots are $-1$ and $\tfrac{5}{2}$; with $b=-3$ and $c=-5$, $b^{2}-4ac=9+40=49$.

point: The formula solves all three. $x^{2}-9$ is a difference of squares, so $x=\pm 3$ by square root. $x^{2}-5x+6$ factors as $(x-2)(x-3)$. $x^{2}+x-1$ has discriminant $5$, so it does not factor over the integers.

stem: A rectangle is 3 cm longer than it is wide and has area 40 cm². Which equation says that?

diag.1: uses the relationship between the sides as though it were the area
diag.2: that is the perimeter, not the area
diag.3: adds the 3 rather than applying it to the length

point: $w(w+3)=40$ becomes $w^{2}+3w-40=0$, which factors as $(w+8)(w-5)$, so the width is 5.

stem: $y=x^{2}-4x+c$. As $c$ increases from 0, what happens where the parabola meets the $x$-axis?

options.v: They stay put and the curve moves up
One stays still and the other moves

diag.0: the curve rises, so the $x$-intercepts close in rather than separate
diag.2: the vertical shift is real, but it changes where the curve meets the axis
diag.3: the parabola is symmetric about $x=2$, so the two roots move together

reveal: The roots are $2\pm\sqrt{4-c}$. They meet at $c=4$ and there are none beyond it.

title: Solutions and $x$-intercepts
body: Solving $f(x)=0$ asks: for which $x$ is the output zero? On a graph the output is the height. So you are asking where the height is zero — where the curve meets the $x$-axis.

stem: A parabola never touches the $x$-axis. What does that tell you about $f(x)=0$?

diag.1: one solution is the case where it touches the axis at exactly one point
diag.2: two solutions is the case where it crosses twice
diag.3: The graph determines it: a parabola that never meets the $x$-axis has no $x$ with $f(x)=0$.

point: To factor $x^{2}+bx+c$ with leading coefficient 1, find two integers with product $c$ and sum $b$; they are the constants in the two factors.
